front: What are the two broad generations the JVM heap is traditionally divided into?
back: The young generation (where new objects are allocated) and the old (tenured) generation (where long-lived objects end up after surviving enough collections).
accepted_answers: The young generation (where new objects are allocated) and the old (tenured) generation (where long-lived objects end up after surviving enough collections).
hint: New objects start in one area; survivors graduate to another.

front: Within the young generation, what are Eden and the survivor spaces used for?
back: Almost all new objects are allocated in Eden; when Eden fills and a minor GC runs, surviving objects move into one of the two survivor spaces, and objects that survive enough of these cycles get promoted to the old generation.
accepted_answers: Almost all new objects are allocated in Eden; when Eden fills and a minor GC runs, surviving objects move into one of the two survivor spaces, and objects that survive enough of these cycles get promoted to the old generation.
hint: Eden is where objects are born; survivor spaces are the waiting room before promotion.

front: What is the key difference between a minor GC and a full (major) GC in terms of scope?
back: A minor GC collects only the young generation and is typically fast and frequent; a full GC collects the old generation (and often the whole heap), is much more expensive, and can cause a noticeably longer pause.
accepted_answers: A minor GC collects only the young generation and is typically fast and frequent; a full GC collects the old generation (and often the whole heap), is much more expensive, and can cause a noticeably longer pause.
hint: Small, frequent cleanups versus rare, expensive, whole-heap cleanups.

front: What does "stop-the-world" mean in the context of garbage collection?
back: All application threads are paused while the collector does its work, so no application code runs (and no requests are served) until that GC pause completes.
accepted_answers: All application threads are paused while the collector does its work, so no application code runs (and no requests are served) until that GC pause completes.
hint: The application freezes entirely for the duration of the pause.

front: What is the core design goal of the G1 (Garbage-First) collector compared to older collectors like Parallel GC?
back: G1 divides the heap into many regions and prioritizes collecting the regions with the most garbage first, aiming to meet a configurable target maximum pause time rather than optimizing purely for maximum throughput.
accepted_answers: G1 divides the heap into many regions and prioritizes collecting the regions with the most garbage first, aiming to meet a configurable target maximum pause time rather than optimizing purely for maximum throughput.
hint: Region-based collection tuned toward a pause-time target, not raw throughput.

front: Why do collectors like ZGC and Shenandoah advertise sub-millisecond pause times compared to G1's tens-to-hundreds of milliseconds?
back: They perform almost all of their marking, relocation, and reference-updating work concurrently with running application threads instead of stopping the world for most phases, only pausing briefly for a small, mostly constant-time step.
accepted_answers: They perform almost all of their marking, relocation, and reference-updating work concurrently with running application threads instead of stopping the world for most phases, only pausing briefly for a small, mostly constant-time step.
hint: Do the heavy lifting concurrently; keep the actual stop-the-world sliver tiny.

front: For a batch job that processes as much data as possible per hour with no user waiting on individual pauses, would you tune for throughput or for low pause times?
back: Throughput, since total work completed per unit time matters more than any individual pause; a throughput-oriented collector can accept longer, less frequent pauses in exchange for spending less total CPU time on GC overhead.
accepted_answers: Throughput, since total work completed per unit time matters more than any individual pause; a throughput-oriented collector can accept longer, less frequent pauses in exchange for spending less total CPU time on GC overhead.
hint: No one is watching a clock for a single request, so optimize total work done.

front: For a low-latency API where every request must respond quickly and consistently, would you tune for throughput or for low pause times, and why?
back: Low pause times, because a single long stop-the-world pause directly becomes a latency spike (or timeout) for whatever requests happen to be in flight, which matters more than squeezing out slightly higher aggregate throughput.
accepted_answers: Low pause times, because a single long stop-the-world pause directly becomes a latency spike (or timeout) for whatever requests happen to be in flight, which matters more than squeezing out slightly higher aggregate throughput.
hint: A user-facing request notices a pause directly; optimize to avoid that spike.

front: What is the difference between java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space and java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace?
back: Heap space exhaustion means regular objects can't be allocated because the configured heap is full; Metaspace exhaustion means the area holding class metadata (loaded classes, generated bytecode) is full, often caused by classloader leaks repeatedly loading classes that are never released.
accepted_answers: Heap space exhaustion means regular objects can't be allocated because the configured heap is full; Metaspace exhaustion means the area holding class metadata (loaded classes, generated bytecode) is full, often caused by classloader leaks repeatedly loading classes that are never released.
hint: One is about instances filling up; the other is about class definitions filling up.

front: What does "GC overhead limit exceeded" mean when it appears as part of an OutOfMemoryError?
back: The JVM detected it is spending an excessive proportion of CPU time doing garbage collection while reclaiming very little heap space each time, indicating the application is effectively out of usable memory even though a full OutOfMemoryError hadn't yet been thrown.
accepted_answers: The JVM detected it is spending an excessive proportion of CPU time doing garbage collection while reclaiming very little heap space each time, indicating the application is effectively out of usable memory even though a full OutOfMemoryError hadn't yet been thrown.
hint: Working almost constantly at GC for almost no benefit is itself treated as a fatal condition.

front: What do the -Xms and -Xmx JVM flags configure?
back: -Xms sets the initial heap size and -Xmx sets the maximum heap size the JVM is allowed to grow to.
accepted_answers: ["-Xms sets initial heap size and -Xmx sets maximum heap size","initial and maximum heap size"]
hint: One is the starting size, the other is the ceiling.

front: Why might setting -Xms equal to -Xmx be recommended for a production service with a known, stable memory footprint?
back: It avoids the overhead and pause behavior of the JVM having to repeatedly resize the heap at runtime, since the heap starts at its full intended size instead of growing incrementally under load.
accepted_answers: It avoids the overhead and pause behavior of the JVM having to repeatedly resize the heap at runtime, since the heap starts at its full intended size instead of growing incrementally under load.
hint: Skip the resizing work by starting already at the size you know you'll need.

front: A service's static field holds a growing List that entries are added to but never removed from. What is this a textbook example of, and why does the garbage collector not clean it up?
back: A memory leak: the objects in the list are still reachable through the static reference, so the garbage collector correctly considers them "in use" and will never reclaim them, even though the application logically has no more use for the old entries.
accepted_answers: A memory leak: the objects in the list are still reachable through the static reference, so the garbage collector correctly considers them "in use" and will never reclaim them, even though the application logically has no more use for the old entries.
hint: Reachable-but-unused is invisible to a garbage collector that only tracks reachability.

front: Why can an unbounded, never-cleared ThreadLocal cause a memory leak specifically in a thread-pooled server?
back: Threads in a pool are reused indefinitely rather than destroyed after each request, so a value set into a ThreadLocal and never removed stays attached to that pooled thread and accumulates across many unrelated requests instead of being cleaned up when the "logical" task ends.
accepted_answers: Threads in a pool are reused indefinitely rather than destroyed after each request, so a value set into a ThreadLocal and never removed stays attached to that pooled thread and accumulates across many unrelated requests instead of being cleaned up when the "logical" task ends.
hint: Pooled threads never die, so anything you forget to clear from them never gets cleared either.

front: What does escape analysis let the JIT compiler do with an object that provably never leaves the scope of a method (never "escapes")?
back: Allocate it on the stack (or eliminate the allocation entirely via scalar replacement) instead of the heap, avoiding garbage collection overhead entirely for that object.
accepted_answers: Allocate it on the stack (or eliminate the allocation entirely via scalar replacement) instead of the heap, avoiding garbage collection overhead entirely for that object.
hint: If an object never leaks out of a method, it may never need to live on the heap at all.

front: Why do microbenchmarks of JIT-compiled Java code need a "warm-up" period before measuring, and what happens if you skip it?
back: The JIT compiler starts by interpreting bytecode and only compiles hot methods to optimized native code after they run enough times, so measurements taken immediately reflect slow interpreted/partially-optimized execution rather than the JVM's steady-state performance.
accepted_answers: The JIT compiler starts by interpreting bytecode and only compiles hot methods to optimized native code after they run enough times, so measurements taken immediately reflect slow interpreted/partially-optimized execution rather than the JVM's steady-state performance.

front: What is the JVM's Metaspace used for, and how does it differ from the old PermGen it replaced?
back: Metaspace holds class metadata (loaded class definitions, method info); unlike PermGen, it is allocated from native memory rather than the Java heap and by default grows dynamically instead of being a small, fixed-size region that was a common source of OutOfMemoryError.
accepted_answers: Metaspace holds class metadata (loaded class definitions, method info); unlike PermGen, it is allocated from native memory rather than the Java heap and by default grows dynamically instead of being a small, fixed-size region that was a common source of OutOfMemoryError.
hint: Same purpose as PermGen (class metadata), different memory area and default growth behavior.

front: What is the difference between a SoftReference and a WeakReference for garbage collection purposes?
back: A SoftReference's referent is only cleared when the JVM needs to free memory (useful for memory-sensitive caches), while a WeakReference's referent is cleared at the next garbage collection cycle as soon as it has no other strong references, regardless of memory pressure.
accepted_answers: A SoftReference's referent is only cleared when the JVM needs to free memory (useful for memory-sensitive caches), while a WeakReference's referent is cleared at the next garbage collection cycle as soon as it has no other strong references, regardless of memory pressure.
hint: Soft references hang on until memory is actually tight; weak references let go as soon as nothing else needs them.

front: Why are finalizers (overriding Object.finalize()) discouraged in favor of try-with-resources or java.lang.ref.Cleaner for resource cleanup?
back: Finalizers run at an unpredictable time (or possibly never), can delay garbage collection, and can resurrect objects, whereas try-with-resources cleans up deterministically at a known point and Cleaner offers a safer, non-resurrecting mechanism tied to reachability.
accepted_answers: Finalizers run at an unpredictable time (or possibly never), can delay garbage collection, and can resurrect objects, whereas try-with-resources cleans up deterministically at a known point and Cleaner offers a safer, non-resurrecting mechanism tied to reachability.
hint: Unpredictable timing and resurrection risk are why finalizers fell out of favor.

back: The JVM caches boxed Integer instances for the range -128 to 127 by default, so small values happen to reuse the same cached object and == passes by coincidence, while values outside that range are freshly allocated distinct objects, making == compare references rather than values.

front: Why is repeatedly concatenating strings with + inside a large loop a performance problem, and what is the standard fix?
back: Each + concatenation on String (which is immutable) creates a brand-new String object, so a loop of N concatenations can allocate roughly N intermediate strings; using a StringBuilder and calling append() in the loop mutates one buffer instead of allocating repeatedly.
accepted_answers: Each + concatenation on String (which is immutable) creates a brand-new String object, so a loop of N concatenations can allocate roughly N intermediate strings; using a StringBuilder and calling append() in the loop mutates one buffer instead of allocating repeatedly.

front: What is a JVM safepoint, and why do stop-the-world garbage collection pauses need one?
back: A safepoint is a point during execution where a thread's state is consistent and safe to inspect or pause (for example, all its object references are in known locations); the JVM must bring every thread to a safepoint before a stop-the-world GC pause can safely begin.
accepted_answers: A safepoint is a point during execution where a thread's state is consistent and safe to inspect or pause (for example, all its object references are in known locations); the JVM must bring every thread to a safepoint before a stop-the-world GC pause can safely begin.
hint: Every thread has to reach a "safe to pause" moment before the whole world can actually stop.

back: More live data in the old generation means every full GC has more reachable objects to trace and more space to compact, directly increasing the time each full collection takes, even though that data is legitimately "in use" and not a leak.
accepted_answers: More live data in the old generation means every full GC has more reachable objects to trace and more space to compact, directly increasing the time each full collection takes, even though that data is legitimately "in use" and not a leak.
